summary.text: The counterexample is $n=800{,}322{,}180$: monotonicity of $B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}$ and $B(16)=1{,}166{,}803{,}110>n$ reduce both binomial indices to $0,\ldots,15$. For every remaining index pair, a finite factorization check shows that $n-B(c)-B(d)$ contains a prime congruent to $3\pmod 4$ to an odd exponent, so the sum-of-two-squares criterion rules out all representations and hence gives $a(n)=0$.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
B(k)=\binom{2k+1}{k}
\]
and put
\[
N=800322180.
\]
We will prove that there are no nonnegative integers \(a,b,c,d\), even without imposing the ordering conditions \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\), such that
\[
N=a^2+b^2+B(c)+B(d). \tag{1}
\]
Consequently the number of representations counted by A303639 is zero at \(N\). Since \(N>1\), this disproves the conjecture that every term with index greater than 1 is positive.

We use the following standard necessary condition for a number to be a sum of two squares.

**Sum-of-two-squares obstruction.** If a prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) occurs to an odd exponent in the prime factorization of a positive integer \(R\), then \(R\) is not a sum of two integer squares.

Here is a proof of the part of the sum-of-two-squares theorem that is needed. Suppose that \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) and that
\[
p\mid x^2+y^2.
\]
If \(p\nmid y\), then \(y\) is invertible modulo \(p\), and \((xy^{-1})^2\equiv-1\pmod p\). But \(-1\) is not a quadratic residue modulo a prime congruent to 3 modulo 4: indeed, if \(z^2\equiv-1\pmod p\), then Fermat's theorem gives
\[
1\equiv z^{p-1}=(z^2)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv-1\pmod p,
\]
because \((p-1)/2\) is odd. This is impossible. Thus \(p\mid y\), and then \(p\mid x\) as well. It follows that \(p^2\mid x^2+y^2\). Dividing by \(p^2\) and repeating shows that the exponent of \(p\) in any nonzero sum of two squares is even. This proves the obstruction.

We next bound the possible binomial indices. Direct evaluation gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrr}
k&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
B(k)&1&3&10&35&126&462&1716&6435
\end{array}
\]
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrrrr}
k&8&9&10&11&12&13&14&15&16\\ \hline
B(k)&24310&92378&352716&1352078&5200300&20058300&77558760&300540195&1166803110.
\end{array} \tag{2}
\]
The values \(B(k)\) are strictly increasing. One quick way to see this is to compare consecutive terms:
\[
\frac{B(k+1)}{B(k)}
 =\frac{\binom{2k+3}{k+1}}{\binom{2k+1}{k}}
 =\frac{(2k+3)(2k+2)}{(k+1)(k+2)}
 =\frac{2(2k+3)}{k+2}>1.
\]
In particular, for every \(k\ge16\),
\[
B(k)\ge B(16)=1166803110>N. \tag{3}
\]
All four terms on the right of (1) are nonnegative. Therefore (1) would force both \(B(c)\le N\) and \(B(d)\le N\). By (3), this implies
\[
0\le c,d\le15. \tag{4}
\]
Thus only finitely many pairs of binomial indices remain.

For each such pair define
\[
R_{ij}=N-B(i)-B(j),\qquad 0\le i,j\le15.
\]
The following table gives, for every unordered pair \(0\le i\le j\le15\), a prime-power obstruction for \(R_{ij}\). An entry \(p^e\) means precisely that \(p\) is prime, \(p\equiv3\pmod4\), and the exact exponent of \(p\) in \(R_{ij}\) is the displayed odd integer \(e\):
\[
p^e\mid R_{ij}\quad\hbox{but}\quad p^{e+1}\nmid R_{ij}.
\]
When no exponent is printed, the exponent is \(e=1\). The row is \(i\), and the labels within that row are the possible \(j\ge i\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|l}
i&\quad j:\text{ obstruction in }R_{ij}\\ \hline

\end{array} \tag{5}
\]

For completeness, the arithmetic content and role of this table are as follows. One first uses the values in (2) to subtract \(B(i)+B(j)\) from \(N\). For the prime in the corresponding entry, repeated exact division gives the odd valuation asserted in (5), and one final division has nonzero remainder; reduction modulo 4 gives remainder 3. Primality is a finite trial-division check by primes no larger than the square root of the displayed number. Thus the table records exactly the data needed for the sum-of-two-squares obstruction, rather than merely giving arbitrary divisors.

For illustration, at \((i,j)=(0,0)\),
\[
R_{00}=800322180-1-1=800322178=647\cdot1236974,
\]
where \(647\) is prime, \(647\equiv3\pmod4\), and \(647\nmid1236974\). Hence its exponent is one. At \((1,1)\),
\[
R_{11}=800322180-3-3=800322174
      =3^3\cdot29641562,
\]
and \(3\nmid29641562\), so the exact exponent is the odd number 3. At \((1,5)\),
\[
R_{1,5}=800322180-3-462=800321715
       =3^7\cdot365945,
\]
with \(3\nmid365945\). These examples also show how entries with and without printed exponents are read; all other entries are obtained by the same direct integer arithmetic. Symmetry \(R_{ij}=R_{ji}\) is why only the upper triangular half is needed.

We now exclude (1). Assume for contradiction that (1) holds. By (4), \(c,d\in\{0,1,\ldots,15\}\). Let
\[
i=\min(c,d),\qquad j=\max(c,d).
\]
Then \(0\le i\le j\le15\), and rearranging (1) gives
\[
a^2+b^2=N-B(i)-B(j)=R_{ij}. \tag{6}
\]
Select the entry in row \(i\), column \(j\), of (5). It supplies a prime \(p\equiv3\pmod4\) whose exponent in \(R_{ij}\) is odd. By the sum-of-two-squares obstruction, \(R_{ij}\) cannot equal \(a^2+b^2\), contradicting (6). This handles every possible pair \((c,d)\), and therefore proves that (1) has no solution in nonnegative integers.

In particular, imposing the additional conditions \(a\le b\) and \(c\le d\) cannot produce a solution. Hence the number of representations of \(800322180\) in the form
\[
a^2+b^2+\binom{2c+1}{c}+\binom{2d+1}{d},
\qquad a\le b,� c\le d,
\]
is zero. Thus
\[
a(800322180)=0.
\]
Since \(800322180>1\), this is a counterexample to the assertion that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\), and the conjecture is false.
